concept.name: Bearish engulfing
concept.definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small white (up) body is followed by a larger black (down) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major top reversal signal because sellers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor.
concept.intuition: After a rising session, sellers hit the market hard enough to open higher and close below where the previous session opened, erasing the buyers' progress in one move.
concept.mechanics: From OHLC data: C1 > O1 (up candle), then O2 > C1 and C2 < O1, so the second real body engulfs the first. Only the bodies must overlap; shadow containment is not required. Follow-through weakness on the next candle is used as confirmation.
concept.formula: Bearish engulfing when C1 > O1, C2 < O2, O2 >= C1, C2 <= O1 (bodies strictly compared per convention).
concept.failure_modes: In strong bull markets bearish engulfing patterns often mark one-day profit-taking before the advance resumes. They are also common noise in sideways ranges where neither direction follows through.
concept.misconceptions: The pattern does not require the second candle's shadows to engulf the first candle's range. And it is not an automatic short signal; context (resistance, volume, prior trend maturity) and confirmation matter.
concept.example: A stock in an uptrend closes at 55.00 after opening at 54.00; the next day it opens at 55.50 and closes at 53.50. The black body engulfs the prior white body, and a lower close the following day would confirm the bearish reading.
